subtopic: Moral Dilemmas, Kohlberg, Virtue Ethics, Deontology, & Utilitarianism

items.definition: Moral standards are norms that govern actions with serious consequences for human well-being, take precedence over other considerations, and are independent of legal authority, whereas non-moral standards are social conventions like etiquette, fashion rules, and grammar.
items.rationalization: A moral standard (e.g., 'Do not murder' or 'Tell the truth') possesses universal validity and overrides etiquette or local legal statutes when they conflict.

mnemonic.title: Moral vs Non-Moral
mnemonic.phrase: Moral = Human Well-Being; Non-Moral = Social Etiquette
items: N - Non-moral: table manners, dress codes

items.tosCompetency: Distinguish moral standards from non-moral standards and etiquette

items.definition: A situation where a decision-maker is faced with two or more conflicting moral obligations, has the ability to choose each one, but cannot fulfill both without violating the other.
items.rationalization: In a true moral dilemma, any choice the agent makes results in a moral wrong or tragedy (e.g., Heinz dilemma or the Trolley problem).

mnemonic.title: Dilemma Conflict
mnemonic.phrase: Two Duties, Impossible to Fulfill Both

items.tosCompetency: Identify and resolve moral dilemmas at individual, organizational, and systemic levels

items.definition: A moral dilemma that arises within institutional, economic, political, or social systems where policies, laws, and organizational structures pit ethical principles against each other.
items.rationalization: Contrast with individual dilemmas (personal choices) and organizational dilemmas (workplace management conflicts); systemic dilemmas involve societal policies (e.g., universal healthcare rationing vs corporate profit).
items.tosCompetency: Identify and resolve moral dilemmas at individual, organizational, and systemic levels

items.definition: The view that moral values, rights, and wrongs are entirely defined and validated by individual cultures, with no universal, objective moral standards applicable to all human beings.
items.rationalization: Philosopher James Rachels critiqued cultural relativism by pointing out that if relativism were true, societies could never criticize slavery, anti-Semitism, or infanticide as objectively evil.

mnemonic.title: Cultural Relativism Trap
mnemonic.phrase: Culture Decides, But Lacks Universal Justice

items.tosCompetency: Evaluate cultural relativism and universal ethical standards

items.term: Kohlberg: Stage 1 - Punishment and Obedience Orientation
items.definition: The earliest stage of moral reasoning (Pre-conventional Level) where an individual decides what is right or wrong solely based on fear of physical punishment and obedience to power.
items.rationalization: A child thinks: 'If I steal the medicine, I will be whipped and put in jail; therefore, stealing is bad.' Conscience is entirely external.
items.tosCompetency: Classify Kohlberg's stages of moral development

items.term: Kohlberg: Stage 2 - Individualism and Instrumental Exchange
items.definition: The stage of moral reasoning (Pre-conventional Level) where actions are judged right if they satisfy one's own immediate self-interest, operating on a 'tit-for-tat' marketplace mentality.
items.rationalization: Governed by the rule: 'You scratch my back, and I'll scratch yours.' Right behavior is defined instrumentally by what serves one's advantage.
items.tosCompetency: Classify Kohlberg's stages of moral development

items.term: Kohlberg: Stage 3 - Interpersonal Conformity ('Good Boy / Nice Girl')
items.definition: The moral reasoning stage (Conventional Level) where an individual acts to gain social approval, please peers, and conform to community expectations of being a 'good' person.
items.rationalization: Motivation shifts from external punishment to peer acceptance and family approval: 'I must do this because I want others to like and admire me.'
items.tosCompetency: Classify Kohlberg's stages of moral development

items.term: Kohlberg: Stage 4 - Law and Order Orientation
items.definition: The moral reasoning stage (Conventional Level) where right behavior consists of doing one's duty, showing respect for established authority, and maintaining social order for its own sake.
items.rationalization: Believes that laws must be rigidly obeyed by everyone without exception, because society would collapse into anarchy if individuals broke rules based on personal discretion.

mnemonic.title: Kohlberg Stage 4
mnemonic.phrase: Uphold the Law at All Costs

items.tosCompetency: Classify Kohlberg's stages of moral development

items.term: Kohlberg: Stage 5 - Social Contract and Individual Rights
items.definition: The moral reasoning stage (Post-conventional Level) where laws are viewed as social contracts designed to protect fundamental human rights, and unjust laws can and should be democratically changed.
items.rationalization: Recognizes that while laws serve social utility, human life and liberty take priority over outdated statutes (e.g., civil rights marches defying segregation laws).
items.tosCompetency: Classify Kohlberg's stages of moral development

items.definition: The highest stage of moral development where an individual follows self-chosen universal ethical principles of justice, equality, and human dignity, even when they violate civil laws.
items.rationalization: Guided by pure conscience (e.g., Mahatma Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela); the individual is prepared to suffer imprisonment or death for moral truth.
items.tosCompetency: Classify Kohlberg's stages of moral development

items.definition: The ancient Greek philosophical concept signifying the ultimate purpose, objective, or end-goal of a human action, living thing, or institution.
items.rationalization: In Aristotelian teleology, everything in nature has an intrinsic purpose (the telos of an acorn is to become an oak tree; the telos of human life is eudaimonia).
items.tosCompetency: Apply Aristotle's Virtue Ethics (Nicomachean Ethics)

items.definition: Aristotle's doctrine that moral virtue is the balanced intermediate state lying between two vices: a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency.
items.rationalization: For example, Courage is the Golden Mean between Cowardice (deficiency of confidence) and Rashness/Foolhardiness (excess of confidence). Generosity is the mean between Stinginess and Extravagance.
items.tosCompetency: Apply Aristotle's Virtue Ethics (Nicomachean Ethics)

items.definition: The intellectual virtue of deliberating well and making sound moral judgments suited to specific, concrete circumstances in real life.
items.rationalization: Virtue ethics requires phronesis because moral rules cannot be rigidly memorized like formulas; one must know how, when, and to what degree to practice virtue in context.

mnemonic.title: Phronesis Clue
mnemonic.phrase: Practical Moral Judgment in Real Life

items.tosCompetency: Apply Aristotle's Virtue Ethics (Nicomachean Ethics)

items.definition: Aristotle's doctrine that moral virtues are not innate by nature, but are acquired and developed through repeated practice and consistent habit until they become second nature.
items.rationalization: 'We become just by doing just acts, temperate by doing temperate acts, brave by doing brave acts.' Moral character is forged through continuous habit.

mnemonic.title: Habit Makes Virtue
mnemonic.phrase: We Are What We Repeatedly Do

items.tosCompetency: Apply Aristotle's Virtue Ethics (Nicomachean Ethics)

items.definition: The ethical framework asserting that moral truth is grounded in human nature and discovered by human reason reflecting on God's eternal design.
items.rationalization: Synderesis is the core natural law precept: 'Good is to be done and pursued, and evil is to be avoided.' All secondary moral obligations flow from this principle.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze St. Thomas Aquinas's Natural Law and Principle of Double Effect

items.definition: An ethical rule in Natural Law that permits performing an action that produces both a good effect and a foreseen evil effect, provided four strict conditions are met.
items.rationalization: The 4 conditions: 1. The act itself must be morally good or indifferent; 2. The good effect must not be achieved by means of the bad effect; 3. The bad effect is foreseen but not intended; 4. Proportionate reason exists.

mnemonic.title: Double Effect Conditions
mnemonic.phrase: Good Act, Bad Not Intended, Good Means, Proportionate

items.tosCompetency: Analyze St. Thomas Aquinas's Natural Law and Principle of Double Effect

items.definition: St. Thomas Aquinas's hierarchy of laws: Eternal Law (God's divine reason), Divine Law (revealed scripture like the Ten Commandments), Natural Law (moral law discovered by human reason), and Human Law (civil laws made by governments).
items.rationalization: Human law is valid only if it accords with Natural Law; an unjust civil law that violates Natural Law is 'no law at all' (lex iniusta non est lex).
items.tosCompetency: Analyze St. Thomas Aquinas's Natural Law and Principle of Double Effect

items.definition: The normative ethical theory pioneered by Immanuel Kant arguing that the morality of an action is based solely on adherence to duty and universal moral rules, regardless of consequences.
items.rationalization: Greek 'deon' means duty. For Kant, an action done merely to achieve a good consequence or out of emotional desire has zero genuine moral worth; it must be done for the sake of duty alone.
items.tosCompetency: Apply Immanuel Kant's Deontology and Categorical Imperative

items.definition: Kant's foundational doctrine that a Good Will is the only thing in the universe that can be conceived of as unconditionally good in itself, without qualification.
items.rationalization: Intelligence, wealth, courage, and health are good only if guided by a good will; in the hands of an evil person, high intelligence makes them a more dangerous villain.
items.tosCompetency: Apply Immanuel Kant's Deontology and Categorical Imperative

items.definition: Kant's supreme moral command: 'Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.'
items.rationalization: If everyone making a false promise to borrow money would cause the institution of promising to collapse, then making a lying promise is a self-contradiction and unconditionally forbidden.
items.tosCompetency: Apply Immanuel Kant's Deontology and Categorical Imperative

items.definition: Kant's second formulation of the Categorical Imperative: 'Act in such a way that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, never merely as a means to an end, but always at the same time as an end.'
items.rationalization: Forbids exploitation, slavery, deceit, and manipulation; respects the absolute dignity, autonomy, and rational agency of every individual.

mnemonic.title: Humanity Formula
mnemonic.phrase: People are Ends, Never Merely Means

items.tosCompetency: Apply Immanuel Kant's Deontology and Categorical Imperative

items.definition: Autonomy is self-governance where a rational agent acts freely in accordance with self-legislated moral laws; Heteronomy is when action is driven by external desires, fears, peers, or laws.
items.rationalization: True moral freedom for Kant is autonomy: overcoming animal impulses and societal pressure to obey the universal moral law of reason.
items.tosCompetency: Apply Immanuel Kant's Deontology and Categorical Imperative

items.definition: The normative ethical theory stating that the morally right action is the one that produces the greatest balance of pleasure or happiness over pain for the greatest number of people.
items.rationalization: Founded by Jeremy Bentham and refined by John Stuart Mill; consequences alone determine whether an action is morally good or bad.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze Utilitarianism (Bentham and Mill) and consequentialist ethics

items.definition: The branch of utilitarianism that assesses each specific, individual act directly by calculating its net pleasure and pain using the Hedonic Calculus.
items.rationalization: Bentham asserted that 'nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters: pain and pleasure.' All pleasures are quantitatively equal ('push-pin is as good as poetry').
items.tosCompetency: Analyze Utilitarianism (Bentham and Mill) and consequentialist ethics

items.definition: Bentham's mathematical algorithm to calculate the quantity of pleasure and pain produced by an act, based on 7 variables: Intensity, Duration, Certainty, Propinquity, Fecundity, Purity, and Extent.
items.rationalization: Extent is the variable that makes utilitarianism social rather than selfish: it counts the number of other persons affected by the action.

mnemonic.title: Hedonic 7 Variables
mnemonic.phrase: I-D-C-P-F-P-E: Intensity, Duration, Certainty, Propinquity, Fecundity, Purity, Extent

items.tosCompetency: Analyze Utilitarianism (Bentham and Mill) and consequentialist ethics

items.definition: The branch of utilitarianism stating that actions are morally right if they conform to general rules that, if universally followed, produce the greatest overall happiness.
items.rationalization: Prevents atrocities permitted by crude Act Utilitarianism (e.g., executing an innocent person to quell a riot violates the rule 'Do not frame innocents', which maximizes long-term trust).

mnemonic.title: Rule Utilitarianism
mnemonic.phrase: Follow Rules that Maximize Long-Term Utility

items.tosCompetency: Analyze Utilitarianism (Bentham and Mill) and consequentialist ethics

items.term: Higher vs Lower Pleasures (John Stuart Mill)
items.definition: Mill's qualitative distinction arguing that intellectual, artistic, and moral pleasures are inherently superior to mere bodily physical pleasures.
items.rationalization: Mill's famous maxim: 'It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.'

mnemonic.title: Mill's Pleasures
mnemonic.phrase: Better Socrates Dissatisfied Than a Pig Satisfied

items.tosCompetency: Analyze Utilitarianism (Bentham and Mill) and consequentialist ethics

items.definition: The libertarian ethical principle from 'On Liberty' stating that the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community against his will is to prevent harm to others.
items.rationalization: Self-regarding actions (even self-destructive ones like smoking or unhealthy diets) are protected; the state may only intervene when third parties are harmed.

mnemonic.title: Harm Principle
mnemonic.phrase: Stop Others from Harm, Not from Self-Choice

items.tosCompetency: Analyze Utilitarianism (Bentham and Mill) and consequentialist ethics

items.definition: A thought experiment in Rawls's Theory of Justice where individuals design principles for a just society without knowing their own social class, wealth, race, gender, or natural talents.
items.rationalization: The veil strips away self-serving bias, guaranteeing that rational parties will choose fair social safety nets and equal rights to protect themselves in case they are the poorest member.

mnemonic.title: Veil of Ignorance
mnemonic.phrase: Design Society Not Knowing Your Place

items.tosCompetency: Apply theories of justice and fairness (John Rawls)

items.definition: Rawls's second principle of justice stating that socio-economic inequalities are permissible only if they work to the maximum benefit of the least-advantaged members of society.
items.rationalization: Contrasts with pure laissez-faire capitalism; higher pay for doctors or entrepreneurs is justified only if it improves public healthcare and life for the poorest citizens.

mnemonic.title: Difference Principle
mnemonic.phrase: Inequalities Must Benefit the Least Advantaged

items.tosCompetency: Apply theories of justice and fairness (John Rawls)

items.definition: A feminist normative ethical theory emphasizing relational interconnectedness, empathy, responsiveness, and nurturing vulnerable persons rather than abstract rules and detached justice.
items.rationalization: Published in 'In a Different Voice' (1982) as a critique of Kohlberg's male-centric stages, showing that women often resolve ethical dilemmas through care and preservation of relationships.

mnemonic.title: Care Ethics
mnemonic.phrase: Relationships and Empathy Over Cold Rules

items.tosCompetency: Analyze feminist ethics and the Ethics of Care

items.definition: The principle of justice concerned with the fair, equitable, and moral allocation of goods, wealth, opportunities, and public burdens throughout a society.
items.rationalization: Addresses how taxes should be levied, healthcare distributed, and education funded; major models include Egalitarianism, Meritocracy, and Rawlsian Maximin.
items.tosCompetency: Apply theories of justice and fairness (John Rawls)

items.definition: A theory of justice that considers proportionate punishment to be a morally acceptable response to crime, balanced against the severity of the offense ('an eye for an eye').
items.rationalization: Focuses on moral desert and retributive accountability; contrasted with Restorative Justice, which focuses on repairing harm and rehabilitating the offender.
items.tosCompetency: Apply theories of justice and fairness (John Rawls)

items.definition: The normative ethical position that moral agents ought to act exclusively in their own long-term self-interest, viewing self-interest as the sole criterion of right action.
items.rationalization: Championed by Ayn Rand (Objectivism); contrasted with Psychological Egoism (the descriptive claim that humans naturally only ever act out of self-interest).
items.tosCompetency: Evaluate egoism and altruism in normative ethics

items.definition: The disinterested and selfless concern for the well-being of others, acting to benefit someone else even at personal sacrifice or disadvantage to oneself.
items.rationalization: Regarded as the antithesis of egoism; forms the moral foundation of philanthropy, selfless rescue actions, and professional codes of ethics.
items.tosCompetency: Evaluate egoism and altruism in normative ethics

items.definition: The ethical act of an employee or insider reporting illicit, illegal, unsafe, or fraudulent practices within an organization to authorities or the public.
items.rationalization: Involves a profound moral dilemma between loyalty to the employer/organization versus duty to public safety and truth.

mnemonic.title: Whistleblower Courage
mnemonic.phrase: Blow the Whistle for Public Good

items.tosCompetency: Apply professional and business ethics to workplace dilemmas

items.definition: A situation in which a professional or public official has competing personal, financial, or familial interests that could corrupt their objective judgment in official duties.
items.rationalization: RA 6713 (Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials) strictly requires public servants to disclose business interests and divest themselves to avoid conflicts.
items.tosCompetency: Apply professional and business ethics to workplace dilemmas

items.definition: The bioethical principle requiring that a patient or research subject voluntarily agrees to medical procedures after being fully informed of the risks, benefits, and alternatives.
items.rationalization: Grounded in Kantian autonomy and the Nuremberg Code; a patient cannot be coerced or kept in the dark about experimental therapies.
items.tosCompetency: Apply bioethical principles to medical dilemmas

items.definition: The practice where a doctor or healthcare authority overrides a patient's wishes or withholds information, believing it is in the patient's best interest.
items.rationalization: Paternalism prioritizes beneficence over autonomy; modern medical ethics strongly rejects paternalism in favor of patient autonomy.
items.tosCompetency: Apply bioethical principles to medical dilemmas

items.definition: Active euthanasia is the intentional administration of a lethal substance to end a suffering patient's life; Passive euthanasia is the withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment allowing natural death.
items.rationalization: Passive euthanasia (such as Do Not Resuscitate / DNR orders or removing a ventilator on brain-dead patients) is widely recognized legally, while active euthanasia remains heavily criminalized in the Philippines.

mnemonic.title: Euthanasia Types
mnemonic.phrase: Active = Lethal Injection; Passive = Withholding Machine
items: P - Passive: Allowing nature to take course

items.tosCompetency: Apply bioethical principles to medical dilemmas

items.definition: The human-centered worldview that considers humans as the central and most significant entities in the universe, valuing nature only in terms of its utility to human survival.
items.rationalization: Blamed by environmental philosophers for ecological destruction; contrasted with Biocentrism (all living things have moral standing) and Ecocentrism (entire ecosystems have intrinsic worth).
items.tosCompetency: Examine environmental ethics frameworks

items.definition: Intrinsic value is value that an entity possesses in itself as an end; Instrumental value is value an entity possesses only as a means to achieve something else.
items.rationalization: In Kantian ethics, human beings have intrinsic dignity, whereas tools, cars, and money have mere instrumental price.

mnemonic.title: Value Types
mnemonic.phrase: Intrinsic = In Itself; Instrumental = As a Tool
items: I - Instrumental: Useful as a tool

items.tosCompetency: Examine environmental ethics frameworks

items.definition: An individual's ability to make moral judgments based on some notion of right and wrong, and to be held morally accountable for their actions.
items.rationalization: Requires rationality, free will, and moral comprehension; normal adult humans are moral agents, whereas infants and wild animals are moral patients (deserve moral consideration but cannot be morally blamed).

mnemonic.title: Moral Agent vs Patient
mnemonic.phrase: Agent = Responsible Actor; Patient = Deserves Care
items: P - Moral patient: Protected but blameless

items.tosCompetency: Define moral agency, responsibility, and moral personhood

items.definition: Actions that are morally praiseworthy to perform, but not strictly morally obligatory or blameworthy if omitted ('going above and beyond the call of duty').
items.rationalization: Examples include jumping on a grenade to save comrades or donating a kidney to a stranger. It is heroic to do, but not a punishable crime if not done.
items.tosCompetency: Distinguish duties from supererogatory actions

items.definition: Moral relativism claims truth depends on culture, individuals, or historical eras; moral absolutism asserts that certain actions are intrinsically right or wrong in all times and places without exception.
items.rationalization: Kant was a moral absolutist (lying is always wrong, even to save a friend from a murderer); consequentialists reject moral absolutism in favor of contextual outcome evaluation.
items.tosCompetency: Evaluate moral relativism, absolutism, and objectivism

items.definition: A famous moral thought experiment where a runaway trolley is heading toward five tied-up people on a track, and a bystander can pull a lever to divert it onto a side track where it will kill one person.
items.rationalization: Utilitarians pull the lever (saving 5 lives at the cost of 1); Deontologists argue pulling the lever makes one an active agent of murder rather than a passive bystander.

mnemonic.title: Trolley Dilemma
items: D - Deontologist: Do not cause death

items.tosCompetency: Analyze classic ethical thought experiments

items.definition: Voluntary actions are performed with full knowledge of the particulars and an internal locus of control; Involuntary actions are performed under physical compulsion or due to non-culpable ignorance.
items.rationalization: Only voluntary actions incur moral praise or blame. An act done at gunpoint (compulsion) or under unavoidable lack of facts (ignorance) mitigates or eliminates moral culpability.

mnemonic.title: Voluntary Criteria
mnemonic.phrase: Knowledge and Free Will Equal Accountability

items.tosCompetency: Apply Aristotle's Virtue Ethics (Nicomachean Ethics)

items.definition: The philosophical doctrine that pleasure (or the absence of pain) is the sole intrinsic good and highest objective of human life.
items.rationalization: Epicurus advocated enlightened hedonism (ataraxia / tranquility of mind and simple pleasures), while Cyrenaics advocated immediate sensory gratification.
items.tosCompetency: Compare historical ethical philosophies (Hedonism, Stoicism, Cynicism)

items.definition: The ancient Hellenistic philosophy teaching that virtue is the only true good, and that happiness comes from accepting things beyond our control with emotional serenity (apatheia).
items.rationalization: Pioneered by Zeno of Citium and practiced by Epictetus, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius; distinguishes between what is in our control (our thoughts and choices) and what is not (external events).
items.tosCompetency: Compare historical ethical philosophies (Hedonism, Stoicism, Cynicism)

items.term: Filipino Ethical Concepts: Utang na Loob
items.definition: The indigenous Filipino ethical concept of an internal debt of gratitude incurred when one receives an unsolicited, life-saving favor, creating an enduring moral bond of reciprocity.
items.rationalization: Described by Virgilio Enriquez as a sacred moral value; can become corrupted into patron-client political dependency when used to excuse corruption or nepotism.
items.tosCompetency: Analyze indigenous Filipino values and ethics (Sikolohiyang Pilipino)
